newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish share list move has no impact-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Swedish share list move has no impact-analysts.

text.p: Swedish companies' great escape from the Stockholm bourse's main A-list to the smaller O-list for tax reasons has no evident impact on share investments, market analysts told Reuters on Friday.
"Companies that have transferred their shares have not noted any negative reactions," Leif Vindevag, head of research at the Stockholm Stock Exchange, told Reuters.
"Swedish shareholders think it's great as they don't have to pay tax and foreigners, who don't pay tax in Sweden, shrug their shoulders. It's just the government that loses."

A new law forces Swedes with wealth exceeding 900,000 crowns ($112,000) to pay 1.5 percent tax on 100 percent of the value of shares listed on the A-list, up from 75 percent, while shares on the O-list remain exempt from tax.
At the same time another law says main shareholders, people holding more than 25 percent of a company's votes, do not have to pay tax for shares listed on the A-list after 1991.

The laws caused 13 companies, several of them family-controlled groups that entered the A-list before 1991, to flee from the A to the O or Over-The-Counter (OTC) lists this summer. They have a total market capitalisation of 120 billion crowns, about five percent of the whole bourse's value.
Many companies are expected to follow suit. About 42 percent of the A-listed groups are considering to move, according to a recent poll by Skandinavisk Opinion AB (SKOP).
The move saves main owners from selling shares to pay wealth taxes that sometimes exceed dividend income, which in turn incurs a 30 percent tax.
Among the migrants so far are fashion retailer Hennes & Mauritz, media group Marieberg, construction group Lundbergs and investment firms Latour and Custos.
"It doesn't seem as if it (the transfer) has an effect," a Stockholm chief dealer said.
"Some fund managers might have instructions not to invest in unlisted companies but many look at other indicators such as the company's size and the share's liquidity."
Small, inexperienced institutional investors can have rules saying they can only invest in shares on the main list, but not large fund groups, Vindevag said.
Fidelity Investments, the world's largest independent investment management group, refrained from commenting on the list transfers but emphasised it only focused on fundamentals.

"We have a bottom-up share picking approach which means that we look at a company's fundamentals when we make investments," said Paul Kafka, executive director of corporate communications at Fidelity.
Swedish funds were not worried by the transfers.
"I don't think it has an impact," said Patrik Tigerschiold, chief investment officer Nordic equities at S-E-Banken Fonder.

"It's the liquidity that affects us and the liquidity has not changed. Maybe less known companies that change lists could attract less attention but for large well-known companies such as Hennes & Mauritz it does not matter at all."
H&M has risen 39 percent to 335.5 crowns since moving on June 10, outperforming a general index advance of 10 percent.
Although other movers have a poorer track record, analysts do not think they would have done better on the A-list.
The government and the Stockholm Stock Exchange seem to be the only unhappy campers.
The government is losing tax revenue -- how much is impossible to calculate -- and has said it is looking into changing the laws while the A-list is losing its quality stamp.
"We think it is unfortunate... as we want the different lists to reflect the companies' quality," Vindevag said. -- Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700 1006 ($ = 7.989 Swedish Crowns)
